narrative: During the 2000s, Black and African women's hairstyles continued to thrive as a celebration of their natural beauty and cultural heritage. The afro, a classic style created by combing out natural growth or using chemical curling products, remained a staple in many communities. Cornrows, a traditional hairstyle in Africa and the diaspora, were also popular, often styled in simple lines or elaborate designs. The natural hair movement, which originated in the 1960s but resurged in popularity during this decade, encouraged people to embrace their afro-textured hair, especially in the workplace. Protective hairstyles like box braids and Bantu knots became increasingly popular as a way to minimize manipulation and exposure of the hair to environmental elements, promoting hair health and self-care. Dreadlocks, or locs, were also worn by some individuals, either naturally or through techniques like twisting or backcombing. These hairstyles not only reflected individuality but also served as a testament to the rich cultural heritage of Black and African communities.
